job.style: a short story where children solve a real problem

response.passage: Rohan and Meera were helping their teacher organize the school stationery cupboard. They found a box of pens and pencils. Meera noted that each pen costs 5 rupees more than a pencil. She wrote the relationship as p = q + 5, where p is the cost of a pen and q is the cost of a pencil. Rohan argued that if they had two equations, they could find the exact costs. They looked at a graph showing two lines representing different sets of prices. One line showed the cost of pens and pencils, while the other represented a bulk discount offer. The lines intersected at a single point, (15, 10), which meant a pen costs 15 rupees and a pencil costs 10 rupees. Rohan noticed that the lines extended infinitely in both directions, covering all possible values, including negative ones if they were dealing with abstract coordinates. He realized that a single linear equation has infinitely many solutions, but a pair of equations with different slopes has only one unique solution where they meet. He carefully checked that the point (15, 10) satisfied both equations, confirming it was the correct solution for the pair. They finished their work, happy to see that the intersection point provided the precise cost for both items.
response.summary: Rohan and Meera use a system of linear equations to determine the individual costs of pens and pencils. They learn that while one equation has many solutions, a pair of intersecting lines provides a single unique solution.
